extracted.intended_audience: general readers, literary critics, and amateur detectives interested in principles of ratiocination and evidence evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for investigating a suspicious death: how to evaluate identity, weigh physical/forensic signs, scrutinize witness statements and journalistic claims, and use collateral facts in reaching conclusions. Emphasizes reasoning principles and caution about common fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine identity of the corpse before proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘it is indispensable that our first step should be the determination of the identity of the corpse with the Marie Rogêt who is missing.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish beyond doubt that the corpse is the missing person before tracing a murderer or accepting rewards/agreements that hinge on that identity; misidentification can render subsequent inquiry moot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for unusual prominences as the best guides to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘it is by prominences above the plane of the ordinary, that reason feels her way... the proper question... is not so much

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume ordinary cases are easy; many plausible alternatives increase difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Because a case is ordinary (not 'outré'), the multiplicity of plausible modes and motives makes elucidation more difficult rather than easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the fallacy that lack of striking oddities means the case is simple; precisely because many modes/motives seem plausible, reason must be more rigorous and discriminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question journalistic/ex parte assumptions and sensational claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The press often 'create[s] a sensation—to make a point—than to further the cause of truth' and may adopt ex parte assumptions (e.g., about the time of the murder) without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat newspaper arguments skeptically, unpack their hidden premises, and do not accept rhetorical or epigrammatic assertions as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fixed, blanket rules about decomposition and floating times
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements like 'drowned bodies... require from six to ten days' are false generalities; the period at which a corpse rises is indeterminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the innumerable modifying circumstances that alter decomposition and buoyancy (seasonal heat/cold, water mineral content, depth, current, body temperament, prior disease, presence of adipose tissue, chemical preservation). Do not rely on a fixed days-to-surface rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between drowned bodies and bodies thrown into water after death
rubrics_metrics.description: Drowned bodies (whose struggles force water into lungs and stomach) differ in specific gravity behavior from bodies thrown in after death; the latter commonly float more readily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lump these categories when reasoning about sinking/rising; cause-of-death strongly affects expected buoyancy behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cumulative corroboration: multiple matching personal items multiply probability of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual traits (small foot, a shoe, a garter, flowers) may be weak alone, but when several match the missing person collectively, they do not merely add—they multiply the probability of identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek concordant, corroborative particulars (clothing, peculiar adjustments like a garter clasp set back, multiple identical flowers) because combined matches can convert probable into near-certain identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hair-based identification must be of a peculiarity, not mere presence of hair
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘No arm is without hair... He must have spoken of some peculiarity in this hair. It must have been a peculiarity of color, of quantity, of length, or of situation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing hair as identifying evidence, specify unusual characteristics (color, length, distribution); vague references to hair are not probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughly examine the corpse for despoilation and personal articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions such as 'Had the body been in any respect despoiled? Had the deceased any articles of jewelry about her person upon leaving home? if so, had she any when found?' were 'utterly untouched by the evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record and compare jewelry, clothing, and other personal effects to detect removal or retention; these facts can be crucial to identity and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify affidavits and alibis because they can be mystifications
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Affidavits of this character are readily made matter of mystification.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independently corroborate statements and alibis (e.g., St. Eustache's whereabouts); do not accept sworn statements at face value without inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confine inquiry to immediately apparent facts—attend to collateral and incidental events
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A vast, perhaps the larger portion of truth, arises from the seemingly irrelevant.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore peripheral occurrences, chance events, and incidental details; allow for serendipity and the unforeseen as potentially decisive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that courts' procedural rules may exclude particular instances that are intellectually valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Very much of what is rejected as evidence by a court, is the best of evidence to the intellect.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the difference between legal admissibility and probative intellectual evidence; in constructing a rational explanation, consider exceptional particulars the court might discount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand physical mechanisms (e.g., effect of cannon-fire) before using them as disproof
rubrics_metrics.description: The firing of a cannon produces vibration that may loosen a corpse from mud or overcome tenacity of putrescent tissue, allowing it to rise, rather than causing it to sink again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze mechanical and physical causes carefully; avoid simplistic conclusions about cause/effect when technical processes are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of simplistic inferences about being seen in public—account for routes, time, and population scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that someone 'could not have passed three blocks without some one having seen her' mistake the difference between a public man's habitual periphery and a perfumery-girl's discursive walks; Sunday morning patterns differ too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate witness probability claims against actual patterns of movement, times of day (e.g., Sunday mornings being less crowded), and the relative scale of an individual's acquaintances versus the city's population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat vague impressions of identity as real impressions but seek corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A man may very well be understood to believe, in a case of this kind, without the ability to advance a single reason for the belief of a second party... Each man recognizes his neighbor, yet there are few instances in which any one is prepared to give a reason for his recognition.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect honest, unarticulated impressions of identity but attempt to corroborate them with specific particulars and objective indicators where possible.
